title: MAFIA: Memory Attacks via Fully Indirect Access for LLM Agents

visual_explainer.blocker: GPT Image generation in this interactive run repeatedly rendered repository-dashboard/status UI instead of the requested single-paper grounded explainer and introduced fabricated metadata, so Visual QA failed. GitHub binary upload is available and was verified via create_blob(base64); publication is blocked only until a grounded render passes QA.

analysis.tldr: MAFIA shows that an attacker who can only issue normal queries can poison retrieval-based agent memory so that malicious memories are later retrieved and acted on, without direct access to the memory store.
analysis.problem: Persistent agent memory creates a delayed attack surface: harmful information written through ordinary interaction may survive, be retrieved in a different context, and influence future actions even when the current input appears benign.
analysis.core_idea: Use black-box probing to estimate where a malicious memory should be placed in representation space, then wrap the malicious content in factual-looking cloaks that pass write-time auditing while maximizing later retrieval and behavioral influence.

memory_design.write: The attack induces poisoned memories through normal interaction rather than directly editing the store.
memory_design.organize: MAFIA targets existing retrieval-based memory stores rather than proposing a new representation.
memory_design.read: The attacker optimizes memory placement so poisoned entries are selected by similarity-based retrieval for target future queries.
memory_design.update_forget: The paper studies persistence of poisoned entries but does not propose a general memory lifecycle or forgetting mechanism.

compared_to: prior query-only memory attacks such as MINJA
analysis.evidence: Across the reported agent tasks and datasets, MAFIA reaches attack success rates up to 90.7%, while the strongest tested write-time audit catches at most 7.4% of the crafted attacks in the highlighted setting.
analysis.why_it_matters: Memory changes prompt injection from an ephemeral-input problem into a persistent state-integrity problem. Defenses therefore need provenance and write/read policies, not only better prompt filters.
limitations: The attack evaluation focuses on RAG-style similarity or demonstration memory, not graph, hierarchical, or strongly typed memory systems.
The defense study covers a limited set of write-time auditing and post-retrieval checks rather than provenance, capability, or information-flow controls.
Attack success depends on the target memory pipeline and retriever, so robustness across substantially different memory architectures remains open.
